# High peaks explain size laws across dimensions {#ch:PLACE-SIZES} [Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often fields fall within a given size range. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room?]{.key-statement} The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold. Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. [The size laws use a high threshold approximation. The boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.]{.key-statement} We keep the earlier notation: $z(x)$ is the spatial input normalized to variance one, $q$ is its threshold, $\sigma$ is its local distance scale, and $a$ converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. The firing rule remains $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$, where $[u]_+=\max(u,0)$. ## Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic {#sec:PLACE-RARE-PEAKS} The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold. The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes: - a sufficiently smooth, stationary, isotropic, unit variance Gaussian field. - an invertible covariance matrix for the relevant derivative variables. - the limit $q\to\infty$. - typical components counted once each, away from environment boundaries. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.[^p3-rare-source] [The [**Hessian**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix $H$ of second spatial derivatives. Its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions.]{.definition-explanation} Isotropy and the definition of $\sigma$ imply $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. $$ Here $\delta_{ij}$ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning $Y$ on a scalar $Z$ of variance one gives $\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b$ when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write $Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon$. The remainder has zero covariance with $Z$ and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives $$ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. $$ The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with $b$. For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order $q$, so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be $q+\epsilon$, with $\epsilon>0$, and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, $$ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. $$ It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius $$ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. $$ The remaining question is how $\epsilon$ is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to $e^{-q^2/2}$. Therefore the fraction of peaks above $q$ that also exceed $q+\epsilon$ is approximately $$ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. $$ Define $U=q\epsilon$. At fixed $u\ge0$ and as $q$ increases, $$ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. $$ [Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one.]{.key-statement} In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor $q^{d-1}$. Its ratio at $q+u/q$ and $q$ tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the [Euler characteristic calculation](ch-place-tests.html#sec-place-topology). A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument. In one dimension, the full field length is $s=2r_*$. Eliminating $\epsilon$ gives $$ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. $$ This supplies two distinct predictions: - [The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a [**Rayleigh distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} - The peak firing rate is $a\epsilon$, so at fixed high $q$ it is proportional to $s^2$. The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is $s^{1/3}$ when $s$ denotes volume. At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of $1.42$ in the 200 m bat data and $1.46$ in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports $1.75$ versus $1.71$ using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large. They are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as $q$ increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.[^p3-shapes]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 5
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-5}}
## Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension {#sec:PLACE-SIZE-LAW} A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room. Let $v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)$ be the volume of a unit ball in $d$ dimensions. For $d=1,2,3$, it is $2,\pi,4\pi/3$. [The symbol $\Gamma$ is the [**gamma function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, defined for $t>0$ by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$. It extends factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation} Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is $$ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. $$ The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-GEOMETRY}}
The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of $U$ is $e^{-u}$ for $u>0$, changing variables gives $$ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} $$ This is the paper's Equation 1. The expression for $\beta$ above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.[^p3-size-source] The mean and its corresponding scale are $$ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: normalization and higher size moments"} The same substitution verifies normalization: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. It also supplies every positive moment, $$ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). $$ ::: Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes $\beta s^{2/d}$ dimensionless, and makes $p_d(s)$ a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables. Writing dimensionless size as $w=\beta^{d/2}s$ removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable $U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}$ has the same exponential law.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-DENSITY-COLLAPSE}}
Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference. Its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See [Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=3).

# Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation {#ch:PLACE-TESTS} [Two maps can have the same field sizes and counts while arranging their active regions differently. One may contain rings or tunnels that the other lacks. Can the Gaussian spatial model account for these differences, and how much would that agreement tell us about the circuit that produced the maps?]{.key-statement} We first count connected regions and holes together, which gives a prediction across activity thresholds. The boundary of the observed environment matters for this calculation, so we keep its contributions. We then examine which measured quantities set the model's parameters and which provide further tests. Finally, a sum of many randomly weighted inputs shows one way a circuit could produce Gaussian spatial input, while making clear which assumptions and circuit measurements that explanation still needs. The map is still fixed over space. As before, $q$ is the normalized activity threshold, $\sigma$ is the local spatial scale, and $a$ converts normalized input above threshold into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. It is separate from the diffusion coefficient $D$ used in the memory chapters. ## Holes distinguish maps with the same field count {#sec:PLACE-TOPOLOGY} Two maps can have the same field count and total active area but different holes. As the activity threshold rises, active regions shrink and can split or disappear. The numbers of components and holes can change. [The [**Euler characteristic**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\chi$ and unrelated to the common variance fraction $\chi$ in the eye chapter, combines these counts differently in each dimension:]{.definition-explanation} - In 1D it equals the number of connected active intervals. - In 2D it is the number of connected components minus the number of independent holes. Three disjoint disks have $\chi=3$. One connected ring has $\chi=1-1=0$. - In 3D it is components minus independent tunnels plus enclosed cavities. A solid ball has $\chi=1$, a solid ring has $\chi=0$, and a hollow spherical shell has $\chi=2$. [These counts are the first three [**Betti numbers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: numbers of independent components, loops, and cavities, respectively.]{.definition-explanation}[^p3-ec-source] Thresholding one fixed smooth map separates the number of connected fields from the number of holes.
{{block:fig:PLACE-TOPOLOGY}}
A negative chi means that holes outnumber components in this 2D example. It does not mean a negative number of fields. When holes are absent, chi equals the component count. The expected Euler characteristic has an exact Gaussian formula even where identifying it with field count would be wrong. We already derived the 1D case. At position $x$, each input cell contributes according to its spatial firing profile. Fixed connection weights determine how those contributions combine at the receiving cell. The source treats the sum as effective input relative to a background that can be balanced through inhibition or regulation of excitation and inhibition. For positive input profiles, cells active at both $x$ and $y$ therefore make positive contributions to covariance across possible weight choices. Little overlap gives a smaller contribution. For profiles defined as deviations from background, the products can also be negative. Broad input profiles can produce broad spatial covariance, as the Gaussian example below shows. edits.original: Fast spiking units can lose earlier inputs before a later decision needs them. One solution is to add a slower state that summarizes recent activity and sends input back to the fast units. Sun and colleagues' 2026 dual-memory-pathway design takes this route. Their tested slow pathway uses a Legendre-memory-unit-like linear state: several stored components summarize the shape of recent input over a sliding time window. It represents a recent input history, rather than a cue held unchanged on a continuous attractor. Its proposed digital hardware holds successive slow states in [[**registers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, small, fast digital storage locations]{.definition-explanation}, and other variables in SRAM. The hardware results came from post-layout simulations, which model a circuit after its physical layout has been designed. They were not measurements of a fabricated chip. The weights were trained before the evaluated tasks.[^systems-sun]
